entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Zhi Dun (支遁, 314–366 CE) was a pivotal Chinese Buddhist monk and philosopher during the Eastern Jin Dynasty, renowned for his sophisticated synthesis of Buddhist Prajñā thought with native Chinese Neo-Daoist metaphysics. Operating within the intellectual circles of the gentry elite, he played a critical role in the sinicization of Buddhism, making its abstruse concepts intelligible and appealing to the Han literati who were otherwise steeped in Xuanxue (Mysterious Learning). His elegant prose and engaging philosophical debates established him as a leading voice in the early transmission of Mahayana Buddhism, particularly in the southern court, transforming it from a foreign import into an integral part of Chinese intellectual life.

Born in Chenliu (modern Kaifeng, Henan province), Zhi Dun became a monk at the age of 25, establishing himself in monasteries near Jiankang (modern Nanjing) and later in Kuaiji. He was a celebrated orator and author, known for his commentaries on key Buddhist sutras, including the *Prajñāpāramitā* texts. His most significant contribution lay in reinterpreting Buddhist *śūnyatā* (emptiness) through the Neo-Daoist concepts of *wu* (non-being) and *li* (principle), thereby bridging two distinct philosophical traditions. He controversially asserted that even the physical attributes of the Buddha, such as his thirty-two marks, were merely outward manifestations of an ultimate formless principle, a view that sparked considerable debate among his contemporaries.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Zhi Dun was a crucial figure in the early sinicization of Buddhism, bridging foreign doctrines with native Chinese thought and thereby ensuring the religion's deep integration into Chinese culture for centuries to come. His work directly contributed to the flourishing of Mahayana Buddhism in China and influenced subsequent philosophical developments.
